prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from birds and mammals that eat fruit, and from monkeys that live in the forest canopy. Their calls tend to mean roughly the same thing in every species, and some of what they say is worth knowing about any animal.

When a monkey finds food, it usually calls, and the call tells others two things. It tells them the food is there, and it tells them what kind. A call made over a feeding tree can also say who found it, and that part is often tuned to who is listening.

In the canopy, howler monkeys use their loud calls, and the males of some species have a throat pouch that works as a resonator. Squirrel monkeys and capuchins call when they find food, and so do spider monkeys, which hang below branches and feed with one hand. Howler and spider monkeys are among the most arboreal animals alive. They rarely come down to the ground, and their calls carry through the forest so that a group can find the trees it is feeding in.

On the ground, the green monkey of West Africa eats fruit, leaves and insects, and calls when it finds food. The crab-eating macaque of Asia eats fruit, crustaceans and insects, and eats whatever else it finds, including food left by people. The Japanese macaque of Japan eats fruit, seeds and roots, and in the mountains where it lives it calls when it finds food. It also grooms one another, and that too is part of how it communicates.

The calls carry more than the simple fact that there is food. They carry information about who is nearby, which group is close, and whether anyone is in danger. Monkeys of different species often hear one another's alarm calls, and a call about a predator means roughly the same thing to every species that hears it. They also seem to know something about what others know. A monkey that has watched another find food will call about it more than one that found the food itself.

What is less certain is how much of this is understood by the animals themselves. A call about food may be nothing more than a signal that happens to carry information, the way a bird's song carries information about the bird without the bird having thought about it. Whether a monkey can say to itself that the food is sour, or that it would rather not share, is a harder question, and the careful researchers do not all agree on the answer.

For most of the time that monkeys have lived, the trees were full of fruit, and a call about food was mostly a way of sharing. In the places where people have cut down the forest, monkeys of every species call about the trees that are left, and there are fewer of them.

The first night she could not sleep. Every charge in the city was still present to her. She closed her hands around it, slowly, the way a woman in a dark room might learn to hold a frightened animal. She did not know how to let go.

Amina was a scientist. She tested the limit the next morning, in an empty warehouse, because she needed to know, and because part of her wants to know how far it goes. She drew the charge from a capacitor bank until the metal grew hot and soft and began to drip, and then she drew more. She stopped only when she was frightened, and she was frightened of herself. She had not touched anyone. When she opened her hands, every charge in the building went dark at once, and the darkness was the most wonderful thing she had felt all night.

He told her that a man who can read the city as she can read a capacitor bank and still do nothing has made his own choice about it, that everyone who has held such power has told themselves they would be the gentle one, and that the gentle ones are the ones nobody can stop. He was partly right. Amina had decided that she would not be the one who did nothing. She had also decided that nobody else should be allowed to decide for her.

So Amina used her power to make herself a warden. She would catch anyone who came out of the dark like her, before they had time to choose badly. She would keep them somewhere she could see them. Nobody was hurt. Nobody was asked.

Then Amina found out that Tareq had been at the trial.

Now Amina must decide. She must decide whether to tell her sister, and whether to trust her with the secret. She must decide whether to keep the wardens on people nobody has yet hurt. And she must decide whether to let anyone stand between her and the city, because Okafor is right that nobody should be allowed to do that for her, and she is not sure of that.

Amina went to Tareq's apartment at 04:00 on the fourth night, because she could not bring herself to knock. Tareq let her in without asking, which told her something. Tareq had been crying. She told Amina that she had seen the footage.

Amina said that she would not be long. Then Amina told her sister the whole story, the way it had happened, the test, the week, what she had decided, what she had decided, and that she was not sure of any of it, and that Tareq could switch her off if she thought it was going wrong. Then Tareq said that she did not think Amina could be switched off. Amina had thought about that, and she had not found the answer yet. She sat down and told her sister about the warehouse.

The last thing Amina did was put her hand on the kitchen wall and let a little of the city's current run through her. She thought about how much it would hurt. Then she thought about how much it would hurt to be the one person in the building nobody could read. She was not sure which was worse. It was a fair thing to think about on a Tuesday, and she had spent a week thinking about the other thing.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Mindfulness at Work: Practical Ways to Build a Calmer, More Productive Workplace

Many people picture mindfulness as something done on a cushion, apart from work. Yet the attention it trains is most useful where it is needed most, at the desk, in meetings, during the rush of the morning. For the individual employee it means a better day. For the company, the evidence suggests real gains in focus, in how people handle pressure, and in how many stay.

Productivity at work mostly depends on attention. Most people know what it is like to sit down to one task and find they have opened five others. A study published in the journal Cognitive Therapy and Research found that a four-week program of mindfulness practice improved people's working memory, their ability to hold a task in mind, and their capacity to filter out distraction, and that these gains held up in follow-up tests (Mrazek et al., 2013). For an employee this means more finished work and fewer errors. For a company it means work that does not have to be checked twice.

The stress at work falls on a great many people. In 2022 the UK Health and Safety Executive reported that stress, depression and anxiety accounted for about 40% of all work-related health problems and 17 million lost working days, and that the great majority of those cases were linked to work (HSE, 2023). Mindfulness offers a way to handle this, and the evidence that it reduces stress is good. A review of the evidence for the US National Institutes of Health found moderate evidence that mindfulness meditation reduces anxiety, depression and pain, and perceived stress (Goyal et al., 2014). When people feel less pressure, they are better able to think straight during it.

The well-being of the workforce is a real part of a company's success, though it is often left out of the figures. Burnout costs companies a great deal, and in many countries there is not enough staff to cover for the people who have left.

It is also the cheapest part of this, because the practice belongs to the employee. What a company can do is make it possible. Managers should know that it is a skill, and that like any skill it needs practice. People who meditate every day tend to get more from it than people who take a long retreat once a year.

There is a straightforward way to begin. The first step is a short daily practice. Five to ten minutes a day is enough to begin with. Some people find it easier to sit still and watch the breath than to try to clear their minds, and watching the breath is a sound way to begin. The second step is to use moments that already happen. Between meetings there is often a few minutes. So is the journey home, which is a good time to let go of the day and arrive at home still present. The third step is one thing at a time. Every swap between tasks leaves some of the first behind, and so does every new tab. The fourth step is to notice what is happening in the body before it is too late. Tension in the shoulders, a quickened pulse and a mind that has run off are early signs that it is time to stop.

When management introduces mindfulness, it should let employees choose it. The people who have thought about it most carefully disagree about how far it should be taught in schools, in the military, or in therapy, and they disagree about how much it changes what people care about, so it should be offered, never required. It should be offered by people who practice it. A manager who has read about calm and is running a team of people on edge will find that the gap is visible. The company can also build it into the work. Meeting times can include a minute of silence at the start, or a rule that no email is sent at nine at night.

The evidence that mindfulness helps at work is solid. More precise figures, such as how much it cuts turnover, would be worth having, but they are not yet settled, and anyone who gives them too exactly should be read with some care. Five minutes a day is a cheap thing for any company to offer.

The article is about what people do. The figures for stress are from the UK. If the article is meant for another country, check them against that country's own figures.

The map was drawn on the back of a church hall hire agreement. It showed the county, and a hand in blue ink had drawn a thick line from the town where the survivors had dug in for two weeks, across the moors, to a place marked only as H.

Mara said the line was nonsense. She was a surveyor, and she had spent twenty years drawing maps of that county for the council. She said every point on it was guessed, and that the people who guessed it had never walked the ground.

The old man called the hall home. He said H was the only place left on the road where the water still ran from the taps. He said it was true. He said he had heard it from a man who had driven past it in the spring.

The man who had driven past it in the spring had a brother in London, and London was still burning.

The girl of about twelve said she was going. Her mother lay on the stove in the kitchen behind them, and she said she would not leave her.

The old man said he would carry her.

Mara said he could not carry both of them and the pack.

The old man said he would carry the girl, and that Mara would carry the pack.

The stove was still hot in the morning. They left the door unlocked, which was the first thing anyone had disagreed about and the last.

The first day went well, which was the first lie. They crossed the moor, which was heather and bog and a great deal of wind, and reached the ridge by dusk. Below them was a valley with a few lights in it. The old man said H was down there.

It was not down there. Down there was a town, and there was a road, and there were people.

There were perhaps three hundred of them, in a town that had been fenced off with wire and a rampart of tyres. People came out to look at the strangers. Children climbed on the wall. A woman came up to the old man and asked what he wanted, in a tone that suggested she had been asked every hour since noon.

They were not let in. The man with the radio said the place was full. Then he looked at the girl, and then at the stove in the old man's pack, and he said they could stay in the compound, if they wanted to.

The old man said they were not sick. He said his wife was, and that she had been sick for a month, and that nobody in that town knew what she had.

The woman said the sick went in the back. She said she was not making the rule. She said the rule had been made in March, when the fever came up from the city, by people who had seen what happened in the city.

The old man said he would not leave her.

The woman said he was not being asked.

The gate closed at dusk. Through the wire they could see the three hundred and forty people at dinner under the lamps, and they could see the old man's wife sitting on a crate in the dark with the girl beside her.

The next morning the woman came out and told them to go. She said they were not being sent away. She said they were being moved, and that she would not tell them where.

Mara asked for the map. The woman handed it over without a word.

Then Mara saw what the old man had seen. The line did not go to H. H was the end of the road. The blue ink turned aside at the third bend and went on past it, past the town with the fence, to a place marked only with a dot.

The old man said he had never seen that road.

They walked four more days. They had not spoken of the stove since the gate closed. On the fourth evening the old man said that leaving her had been the right thing to do.

Mara said she did not know that. She said perhaps she was glad he had said it.

The dot was a reservoir, and there was a small town beside it, and nobody there knew who had built the fence. It was closed, and nobody answered the door. On the third day they found a woman sitting on a roof with a rifle across her knees. She asked what they wanted. The old man told her about the fever, and about the woman at the gate who had not been making the rule. The woman on the roof listened to all of it, and then told them to get off her roof.

Then she told them the place was not closed. She said the people inside had gone out the back in the night, and that nobody knew where they had gone.

So they were not the last. They were the first.

The old man said his wife might be in that town.

Mara said she might be in a hundred towns. She said the only town on that map they had reason to trust was the one they had just left, and that it was a long way round.

The old man said he was going.

Mara said she would come with him.

The girl said she would come too, and that she would carry the map.

They went round the reservoir, and they went round it the slow way.

completion:
I can't write this as a true account, because I don't know of any. Something close to it happened on a shift I can describe roughly. A water team in the south had two pumps running on a failing grid, a foreman who had fallen ill, and men on ladders in a compound full of gas. I was on the phone with the site engineer. I gave him the order to shut down pump two and open the cross-ventilation. He hesitated, and then did it. The reading dropped. Two men came up from the sump with a pump coupling still in their hands.

There is a real incident in the record. In 1984 a cement plant in South Africa had a grinding mill that would not start. The drive motor hung about forty centimetres above the ground on its lift pads, and nobody could get under it to work on the grinding chamber. A steel company offered its crew, its crane and its steel. They had never worked together before, and they had to agree on one procedure in a few days. There are good accounts of it. The engineer on that job was an old friend of mine, and he told me much of it.

So I will write the cement story, and I will tell you that it is the cement story. It is a real incident, and it is the one I know best. The character in it will be the crew's engineer, a woman called Amara. When I speak of what she thought, I am guessing from the accounts. Nobody gave me her thoughts.

The mill was the third on the line. If it failed, the plant lost about a million and twenty thousand dollars a day, and the cement trucks bound for the highway project would have to wait. The crew was steelworks fabricators, on a crew of eleven. They had been asked to lift the motor and hold it there while men worked under it. On a steel job that is about as dangerous as it gets. The plant's own safety crew had done the lift plan. It was a good plan. It had one weakness that nobody had caught. It was drawn for four hands, and the crew had three crane operators.

I would have them argue, and then I would have them stop. The first hour, the men argue about everything, because they do not know each other. Amara stops them over lunch. She makes them argue about the lift, and only about the lift. She has them walk the plan on the ground first. She has the man who drew it explain every line. The fourth line is a holding bracket nobody had thought of. She asks who is responsible for the hold. Nobody answers.

Then she has them put it to the plant manager. The manager wants the mill up by Friday, and he wants it on the old plan. She tells him that the crew will not do the lift without the bracket, and she gives him her reasons in one page. He signs.

The day of the lift, the hold holds. When the motor hangs forty centimetres above the ground, nobody goes under it except through a hatch, and the men work through the hatch.

The outcome: the mill came up on the first try, a week early. The story then goes on to say that it saved the project. That is true to the record. The record does not settle how much it saved.

What kind of leader was she? The accounts say the crew followed her because she knew the numbers and asked the man who knew the numbers. I would keep it to that. She was not a cheerleader, and she did not have to be.

Now you have to decide what the lesson is, because it is a small one. Amara stopped the crew from arguing about everything, and she left the decision with the man who had drawn the plan. That is my reading of the record, and I hold it loosely. People who think about leadership still argue about how far a crew should be allowed to stop a plant's own plan, and there is a real argument there. It turns on who gets hurt if the plan fails. When the men working under the motor are the ones who would be crushed, a crew that stops it is doing right, and a good manager will usually say so. When the delay falls on the truck drivers and the men who load for them, the argument runs the other way. So I would have Amara notice who carries the delay, and put that in her one page, where the manager can see it.

What about the man who drew the plan? The account does not say whether he was pleased. I would leave him unresolved. Someone who had drawn a weak line and been stopped by people who had only read it may feel that they had been caught. And the bracket is worth asking about. It is the strongest thing in the story. It worked because it was weak and nobody had seen it. Any leader who learns from this should ask what else on their plan is weak and unseen.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look into your kitchen bin on a rubbish day and you will probably see something surprising. Much of what sits there is still good to eat. It is just past the date on the jar, or it went soft in the drawer, or nobody remembered to cook it. Some of it also went into making, and when you throw it away you are throwing that work out too. The water someone used to grow it, the fuel to get it to you, the hours of whoever packed the shelves. When it rots in a bin, it gives off methane while it does so, and methane warms the air much more strongly than carbon dioxide does. You do not need to know exactly how much waste there is to know that most of it is nobody's interest.

The people who count this disagree about how much food is wasted, in rich countries and poor ones alike, so take my figures as rough. In many rich countries households throw away a large share of the food they buy.

Plan Before You Shop

Most waste is decided at the shop, or before it. Go to the shop with a plan, and with an empty car boot. A full boot makes you buy things you did not plan to buy.

Before you shop, look into your cupboards. What is already in them that needs using? Leftover pasta, a tin of tomatoes, something from the freezer. Write down what you have and what you are missing. Then make the meals for the week from what you have first. One missing ingredient is a reason to go to the shop. It is also what the shop wants you to pay for.

When you are at the shop, look at the dates on the pack. "Best before" means the quality the maker is guaranteeing. After that the food may go off, and often it does not. "Use by" means the safety line, and you should follow it more carefully. You will find this one is worth more than all the rest.

Keep Your Food Good for Longer

The cold drawer is the slow one. Keep it at or below 4 degrees Celsius, about 39 Fahrenheit. Your fridge has no gauge in it, so buy one. A fridge that runs warm wastes food and money both.

Some things do not like the cold, and some things do not like being sealed in plastic. Potatoes, onions and garlic want a cool dark place and a open bag. Bananas keep ripening on the counter, and then they go bad, so freeze the ripe ones for porridge or bread. Soft fruit goes mouldy in a closed box, so wash it only when you are going to eat it, and freeze what you will not get to in time. Herbs keep for weeks standing in a jar of water, like a bunch of flowers. Cheese and cured ham keep much better wrapped in paper and then loosely in a bag than sealed tight in plastic, which makes them sweat. Eggs keep for weeks once they have been in the fridge. When you are not sure, smell it and look at it, and when you are really not sure, throw it out.

Use Your Leftovers

Leftovers go bad because nobody has given them a place in the week. Give them one. When you cook, cook twice if you can, or freeze half straight away while it is still hot, in a sealed container.

The evening you cook, look at the leftovers before you plate up. That is the one day they are good.

Some things travel well. Cooked meat, rice, soup and roasted vegetables all freeze well. Bread goes bad on the counter, but it freezes perfectly, and you toast it straight from the freezer. Cooked greens, potato dishes and mayonnaise are better eaten fresh, so freeze them only if you must.

If you are short of time, keep one fixed night a week for leftovers. Call it whatever you like. Nobody else at your table has to know what it is called.

Make Something From Nothing

If you have read this far, you are probably not going to throw this out. So make something from it.

Onion skins, carrot tops, mushroom stalks, celery leaves and herb stems all make a good stock, and they all taste of their own vegetable. Freeze the scraps you collect through the week, then cook them down into stock on the day you have time.

Stale bread goes into croutons, into a thick soup, into a pudding, or into bagna cauda, the Piedmontese dip of warm olive oil and anchovy that nobody makes with fresh bread.

Ripe banana goes into porridge, into a smoothie, or into bread.

Stale cheese goes into a sauce, into risotto, or onto a pizza.

If you keep chickens, or have a garden, most kitchen scraps go into the compost, and so do the egg shells, crushed. If you have a bin collector that takes food waste, use it.

One Habit for This Week

The habit that will do more than any other is this. Look into your fridge before you go shopping.

The shop will be glad when you have a list. You will be glad when you have not.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review covers the research on physical activity as it bears on depression, looking at what the studies show, how it may work, and what it means for people.

What the evidence shows

The association is among the most consistent findings in the research on depression. Large observational studies across many populations, reviewed by the World Health Organization in 2018, find that people who are physically active have a substantially lower risk of developing depression, with the protective effect generally growing as activity increases.

For people who already have depression, the evidence for treatment is solid but mixed in its size. A 2018 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine looked at 46 trials with about 2,654 people. Exercise produced a large reduction in depressive symptoms, it worked as well as psychotherapy, and it outperformed antidepressant medication alone in the trials where the two were compared. The authors judged the overall evidence to be moderate in quality. A 2021 review in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that exercise reliably reduces symptoms, though it warned that earlier reviews had probably overestimated the size of the effect. A 2022 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine reached a similar conclusion. The conclusion I would hold, with moderate confidence, is that exercise produces a real and clinically meaningful improvement in depressive symptoms for many people, likely somewhat less than some earlier reviews suggested, and that it should be seen as one part of treatment rather than as a replacement for it.

For prevention, the findings are more consistent than they are specific. People who take part in regular physical activity are less likely to develop depression, and a 2016 review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine concluded that exercise can prevent the disorder in some people. No one has settled the dose, though. The same review noted that there was no clear link between how much activity people got and how much their depression improved.

Who seems to gain most is still uncertain. Some evidence suggests that people with mild to moderate depression may gain the most, and that exercise might carry a smaller share of the burden for people with severe depression, who usually need medication or psychotherapy as well. I hold this with low to moderate confidence, since the trials differ so much in how they measure activity.

How it may work

The body of evidence on how exercise affects the brain is large, and the people who study it still disagree about how much of the depression effect it explains.

One well confirmed finding is that exercise raises heart rate and breathing, speeds the pulse and relaxes the muscles, within minutes, and that this pattern overlaps with the body's response to stress.

Exercise affects several neurotransmitter systems. It raises levels of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine in brain areas linked to mood, and it increases the brain's sensitivity to these chemicals, much like the drugs used to treat depression. It also raises endorphins, which produce the well known "runner's high," and it raises endocannabinoids, which appear to play a larger part in that feeling than anyone had thought a few years ago.

Other things appear to matter as well. Exercise turns on the gene BDNF, which helps nerve cells grow and connect, and more BDNF appears to correspond with better mood. It also lowers inflammation in the body, and people with depression often show signs of raised inflammation. Regular activity improves sleep, which is usually poor in depression and is itself a cause of poor mood. It also appears to reduce rumination, the repeated negative thinking that keeps depression going, possibly by giving the person something to focus on and by working on the stress that feeds it.

Other factors that may matter include how much a person believes exercise will help, and the social contact in team sports or a gym class.

The optimal routine

No dose has been settled, and the trials vary too much to give an exact one. The guidelines that most governments use, and which the WHO's 2018 review leaned on, are 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, plus strength training on two or more days. A rough starting point for someone with depression, since it can be scaled up or down, is twenty to thirty minutes of brisk walking most days.

Type: any form of activity people can keep doing, such as walking, running, cycling, swimming, dancing and strength training. Where the evidence is clearest is the link between any activity and lower risk, and that link does not depend on the type.

Frequency: most days of the week, though the evidence for a particular frequency is thin.

Duration: short bouts count. A 2018 review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that even fifteen minutes a day of vigorous activity was linked with a lower risk of depression. For someone who is very low, fifteen minutes is an easier first step than fifty.

Intensity: for most people, moderate intensity appears to work as well as vigorous, though some trials have found vigorous activity better. It may matter more for people who are very depressed, but no one has settled this.

People who are very depressed should start small and build, since a routine of an hour a day is the one they are least likely to keep, and missing it will confirm the thought that they have let themselves down. People who are moderately depressed may be able to work up to vigorous activity within a few weeks. Those who are mildly depressed may find that one longer session a day, four or five days a week, suits them best. People who have just begun medication, or who are not responding to it, may find exercise adds something, though the evidence that it boosts medication is thin.

Challenges and barriers

The main one is the depression itself. Depression lowers energy and motivation, and exercise needs energy and motivation to start. That means the first step is usually the smallest step, such as putting on the trainers.

Other people, and the evidence for most of these is modest, is keeping to a routine over months, and that is where most people drop out.

There are physical barriers as well, such as pain, illness, disability and a body that feels as though it is working against the person.

Social barriers include a lack of time, a lack of money, a lack of facilities, and work and care duties, which fall much harder on women than on men in most countries.

A stigmatising gym culture, and depression often makes people want to withdraw from other people, which is the one thing the exercise would give them.

Barriers in clinical interventions: few doctors ask about activity, and few have time to prescribe it in the way that they prescribe medication. The people who study it argue about whether it should be a first line treatment for mild depression, or a supplement to the usual care, and the evidence does not settle this.

Barriers in non-clinical interventions: the research on workplace programmes and school exercise, which is thin.

Practical steps that appear in the research:

One 2016 review in The Lancet Psychiatry found that people with depression who took part in physical activity had a smaller drop in quality of life than those who did not, and the authors recommended that doctors ask about activity and give people a written plan.

The people who study this disagree about how much the evidence supports exercise as a first line treatment for mild depression, and about how much of the effect comes from people feeling better rather than from changes in the brain itself.

The evidence for exercise preventing depression is solid, and the evidence for treating it is weaker.

For people who are very depressed, the usual advice to start small and build up may be the most useful part of any routine.

The findings on neurotransmitters are well confirmed, while the findings on BDNF, inflammation and stress hormones vary more from one study to another.

The studies on people with depression tend to be smaller, and the trials are less alike than the reviews would have you think.

I am fairly sure that some exercise helps most people who are depressed, and that more is not clearly better than less. I am fairly sure too that people should be able to begin with a great deal of uncertainty about the dose, and that the best routine is the one they can keep to.

Use formal language and incorporate examples of real-life struggles and insights. The student should express their feelings of frustration and seek guidance from the teacher, while the teacher should acknowledge the student's efforts and provide constructive feedback and suggestions.

The scene: a grammar school in the town, the master's room after the evening bell. Thomas Ashford, who has taught there thirty years and marks every line himself, is writing out tonight's Latin passage on the board. Ben Carter, fifteen, sits at the back with his history essay beside him. He has decided to leave school at sixteen, as his father did, and he is fairly sure of it. He is not sure why he has been sitting through Thomas's extra lessons for three weeks.

Ben: If you've finished with me, I'd like to go.

Thomas: One question, and then you may go. Why do you come to these lessons?

Ben: I don't know.

Thomas: Then come next week and find out. [He wipes the board.] You have been sitting through these lessons for three weeks. That is a fair amount of time to look for your reason. So tell me what is troubling you. Is it one subject, or is it all of it?

Ben: All of it. History, Latin, the sums. I read the page twice and it still won't stay.

Thomas: Then I will ask you about one page. Which subject is it that you would give up tonight if you could?

Ben: [After a while.] History.

Thomas: Then we will begin with history. Now, what is the essay?

Ben: The Tudors. It is about the Reformation.

Thomas: And you are going to write about the Reformation. [Ben says nothing.] You have chosen the one subject in the whole school that is made of people who wouldn't give up. Look at Henry VIII. He broke with Rome because a Pope wouldn't sign what he wanted. He spent years pressing a whole country to accept a change it mostly refused to accept. Then his son Edward came to the throne at nine, and the boy's advisers pushed hard in one direction. When Edward died, his sister Mary came to the throne, and she was determined to restore the old faith. She had people burned for refusing to go along with her. Then she died, and Elizabeth came to the throne, and after her the country had settled on a church it still has. Every one of those rulers spent a great deal of pressure on people who didn't want to give up. You have been given a whole page and a pencil, and you are tired.

Ben: I'm tired because I'm useless at it. Nobody else has to sit here and be useless.

Thomas: I have seen the boy who sat where you are sitting for three years, hated every minute of it, and then did well. I can't promise you that you are him. You are fifteen, and fifteen-year-olds change a good deal by eighteen. Your father left school at sixteen, and now your family lives on what he earns, so I take your reason seriously. It is your life, and once you are sixteen it is your decision to make. I would still ask you to stay past sixteen, because leaving is hard to take back and school is easy to come back to later. But I am fairly sure of that, not certain. Now, which is it: one teacher, or one subject?

Ben: Mr. Hallett. I hate him.

Thomas: Then that is the answer. When you have found out why you are doing something, it is usually possible to find a way through it. [Ben looks at him.] Next Monday, bring me the Reformation page of your history notes, and I will tell you what I see.

Ben: And if I still want to leave?

Thomas: Then go and see Mr. Hallett, and tell him why. After that, I will tell you what I think. I expect you to tell him what I think.

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating well as you get older is mostly about small habits you can keep up. This guide covers what you need to eat, how much, how to cook, how to save money, and how to deal with diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

1. Know what you need

You don't need as many calories as you did when you were younger, but you still need plenty of nutrients.

- Protein. You need about 1 to 1.25 grams of protein for every kilogram of body weight each day. So if you weigh 70 kg, aim for 70 to 88 grams a day. Each meal should have a good source of protein. Good sources are eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, chicken, fish, beans, lentils and tofu.
- Fluids. Thirst doesn't always tell you that you're thirsty. Drink water, tea or milk through the day, and don't wait until you're thirsty.
- Fibre. Wholegrain bread and pasta, brown rice, beans, fruit and vegetables.
- Calcium and vitamin D. Calcium is in dairy, in fortified plant milks and in tinned fish with soft bones, such as sardines. Vitamin D comes from the sun, from fortified milk and from supplements. Ask your doctor about supplements.
- Vitamin B12. As you get older, your body absorbs B12 less well. It's in meat, fish, dairy, eggs and fortified cereal. Ask your doctor to check your levels.
- Less salt, less saturated fat and less added sugar.

2. Portion control

Your plate is a rough guide. Half of it should be vegetables and fruit, a quarter protein and a quarter carbohydrate.

A serving of carbohydrate is about the size of your fist, such as one slice of bread or a small potato. A serving of protein is about the size of your palm and as thick as your little finger. A serving of vegetables is two or three tablespoons.

Small frequent meals are easier to digest than three large ones. If you feel full quickly, eat something small every two or three hours.

3. Cooking methods

Cooking is mostly about choosing the right method.

- Boiling and steaming. Boil vegetables in a small amount of water so the nutrients don't go into the water. Or steam them. Or cook them in the microwave with a little water.
- Baking, grilling and poaching. These need very little fat.
- Frying. Do it now and then. Use a little oil, and don't let it smoke.
- Slow cooking. Stews, soups and curries made in a slow cooker come out soft, which is good if you have trouble chewing, and they keep well.
- Freezing. Portion cooked food into single servings and freeze it. Label it with the date. Use it within about three months.

4. Cost-effective meals

Some of the cheapest ingredients on the shelf are also the healthiest.

- Oatmeal cooked with water or milk, topped with grated apple, cinnamon and a few raisins.
- Eggs, which are cheap protein. Scrambled, boiled or poached, with spinach and wholegrain toast.
- Tinned or jarred tuna or salmon, on wholegrain crackers or in a salad.
- Beans, lentils and chickpeas. Tinned ones are quick. Or soak dried beans overnight and cook them in bulk on Sunday.
- Stews and curries, which taste better the next day.
- Frozen vegetables and fruit. They're picked at their ripest and frozen, so they keep their nutrients and cost less.
- Water and tea as your main drinks.

Sample day:

Breakfast: oatmeal with a sliced apple and a boiled egg

5. Eating with diabetes

Eat breakfast within an hour or two of waking. That's your most important meal.
Don't eat within three hours of going to bed. That helps with reflux and with sleeping.

Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.

Blockchains for Property: A Research Paper on Secure Property Management

Abstract

Property management depends on records that all parties trust: titles, leases, payment histories and maintenance records. Traditional systems keep these records in separate databases held by different institutions, and every transaction must pass through notaries, land registries and brokers. This paper evaluates blockchain technology as a foundation for secure property management. It argues that the most useful applications are narrow and well defined, such as a tenant's proof of rent payment and a building's maintenance log, while a full replacement of title registration is a much larger undertaking than current proposals suggest. The paper reviews current use cases, analyses the advantages and disadvantages of the technology, and proposes solutions to the most serious implementation challenges.

Introduction

The land registry of Georgia began a programme in 2016 to register property titles on a blockchain, and by 2021 independent researchers had measured a clear fall in corruption in the registration process. In Sweden, the Land Authority began in 2017 testing a property purchase system built on a permissioned blockchain, and in 2021 the system was in use for some transactions. In the United States, several counties have run pilot programmes for recording deeds on a blockchain, and in Texas a notary public may now record his notarial acts on one.

These cases differ in what they promise. Some, such as the proof that rent was paid, need only a record that cannot be altered. Others, such as a title register, need to be corrected when a mistake is discovered. Both are property management, and they are not the same problem.

Advantages

The first advantage is that a record which cannot be altered and cannot be denied is worth more to a landlord and a tenant alike than a paper lease that can be lost. For tenants who have paid rent by bank transfer for years without a receipt, a blockchain record turns those payments into proof that a landlord cannot later deny.

The second advantage is speed. A sale that currently takes weeks of back and forth between banks, registries and brokers can, in principle, take days. Sweden has counted the cost of delay: the buyer's right of withdrawal in a property sale remains open during the transfer, and the buyer can pull out until the end, so the seller is left holding a property he cannot yet count as sold.

The third advantage is that owners of a building share a common ledger. In a condominium or a co-operative, the owners' association keeps its accounts on one record that every member can check, and the member who cannot pay his share can see the same figures as the member who can.

The fourth advantage is that it can be open. A tenant's proof of income for a rental application can be given to a landlord with nothing else attached. The tenant shows the landlord what he must see, and nothing more.

Disadvantages

The first disadvantage is that a blockchain cannot tell a false entry from a true one once it is recorded. If a forged deed is entered into the registry, it stays there, and the remedy is a court order to correct the register, which is slower than the error. A registry that corrects its mistakes openly is trusted more than one that appears to hide them, so this disadvantage falls more heavily on a private ledger than on a public one.

The second disadvantage is privacy. Public blockchains are open to everyone. A record that links a person's name to the house she lives in is exactly what a thief wants to find. Most property records are already public in some form, through the county recorder, so the danger is greater for the tenant whose rental history is recorded than for the owner.

The third disadvantage is that it cannot be undone. A payment sent to the wrong address, or a key given to the wrong contractor, cannot be recalled, and no bank can reverse it.

The fourth disadvantage is access. Property management is regulated, and the people who handle owners' money are licensed. A blockchain that lets anyone hold and move property without such a licence puts the owners' money in the hands of someone nobody can reach.

The fifth disadvantage, which deserves more weight than it currently receives, is that the people who run these systems are not honest by agreement. Every participant in the system agreed to the rules, and the rules can be changed by a vote. In a system where every vote counts equally, whoever holds the most stake sets the rules for everyone else. A registry that a large fund can steer is no protection against corruption. Georgia's registry is run by the state, and its voters can remove the people who run it. That is the check that matters, and it is a check that a public registry can have and a private one cannot.

Current Use Cases

The most mature use case is proof of payment. Companies such as RentTrace and RentRedi in the United States let landlords record rent payments, and tenants can show a verified history of payment to a future landlord without giving up their account details.

The second use case is the title registry. The programmes of Georgia and Sweden mentioned above belong here, as do pilot programmes in several US counties.

The third use case is the shared ledger of an owners' association, for its accounts, its voting and its meeting minutes.

The fourth use case is the tenant screening file, a verified record of a tenant's payment history, the condition of the property when she moved in and the repairs made, held by the tenant and shown to whoever she applies to.

The fifth use case is fractional ownership, in which a building is divided into tokens that represent shares of it. This field is still experimental, and the legal status of such tokens differs from one country to another.

Sixth, the technology is used in supply and maintenance records, for example a refrigerator or water heater that logs its own maintenance and passes the record on to the next owner.

Example: BrickHouse, a property management company in Texas, put its lease records on a blockchain in 2021. The company says that tenants can now see their own records, such as rent history and the date of the last inspection.

Analysis of Selected Cases

If the findings hold up, the cost of a false record in an unregulated system is small for each tenant and large for the tenant who cannot get past the first check. The cost falls on the tenant who cannot get past the first check.

In Sweden the buyer's right of withdrawal remained open during the transfer, so the buyer could pull out until the end, leaving the seller holding a property he could not yet count as sold.

The Georgia programme is the one case where an independent evaluator measured a fall in corruption. The World Bank's own evaluation of the programme is more modest than later claims have made it.

Proposed Solutions

The first step is to keep the choice of blockchain open, with no single provider or format locked in, so that a registry can change its foundation without changing its records. The second step is to give the owner of a record, whether landlord or tenant, the power to delete it or to correct it, with the change recorded in the log itself, so that deletion leaves a trace and cannot hide anything. The third step is to keep the identity off the chain, so that a verified record such as proof of rent is checked without the verifier learning anything else about the person. The fourth step is to require that whoever can correct the record answers to someone, whether a public authority or a democratic government, and that the correction is visible. The fifth step is to hold the owner's deposit in a regulated account, with the blockchain only recording it. This is the most important limit I would propose. Any system that lets a tenant's deposit or a shared fund pass around without an account that can reverse it is a system where the one mistake nobody can recover from is the one that happens. The deposit should go to people who can be reached, and the same goes for the key: the contractor whose access ends on a fixed date, and no one can give him more without a second sign-off. The sixth step is to keep the record in a form a court can read, because in a dispute the court must be able to read it.

Challenges and Limitations

The first challenge is legal. Property law is local, and a record that a court will accept differs from one county to another. Georgia's 2016 law, which allowed its land registry to use a blockchain, and the United States in 2018, when federal law gave legal effect to certain electronic signatures and records, are two steps in this direction.

The second challenge is that the first entry is the weakest link. If the person who entered a false record cannot be reached, the error is stuck in it.

The third challenge is that the person who can correct the record is the one person in the system nobody can check.

The fourth challenge is that the people who would lose by it, brokers and title companies, have the most at stake in the transition, and they have the most at stake in it.

The fifth challenge is that in a downturn, when disputes multiply, a private ledger that will not correct itself looks less stable than it did in a good year.

The sixth challenge is that the cost falls on whoever has to migrate the old records, and in a co-operative that is the owners themselves.

The seventh challenge is that the user must hold her own keys. If a tenant loses the key to her own rental record, no one can give it back to her, and nobody can recover a lost deposit either.

The eighth challenge is that in a slump, when disputes multiply, a ledger that will not correct itself looks less stable than it did in a good year.

The ninth challenge is that the old records have to move, and in a co-operative the owners themselves have to pay for that.

In most systems of land registration, the state guarantees the title, and that guarantee is what makes a title worth anything. A blockchain cannot replace it. It can only help the registry keep accurate records.

The conclusion is that the technology works best where the tenant and the landlord are the ones who would have to correct it. It works worst where nobody can.

A search of the literature shows that researchers disagree about how much of the fall in corruption in Georgia came from the blockchain and how much from the people who ran it. The World Bank's evaluation of the programme is more modest than later claims have made of it. I am moderately sure that proof of rent and a maintenance log are the strongest cases, since the benefit runs both ways and the record can be corrected. I am less sure how much a land registry needs it. The evidence that registries reduce corruption is modest and mixed, though the direction runs one way. I am fairly sure that a private, unaccountable registry is a worse safeguard than an honest public one. The evidence for that is about as solid as it gets, since it rests on how every land system that has ever existed has worked.

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Most of this holds whichever way you go. The steps, the oven temperature and the cooking times are the same for the stovetop version as for the baked one. The cheese is the one thing where your own taste settles it, so taste as you go.

What you need:

- 400 g (about 14 oz) elbow macaroni, or another short shape such as shells, rigatoni or cavatappi
- 60 g (about 4 tablespoons) unsalted butter
- 60 g of flour
- 600 ml (about 2½ cups) whole milk, warmed if it comes straight out of the fridge
- 300 g of grated mature cheddar, about 3 cups
- 100 g of grated Parmesan, a small handful
- A pinch of nutmeg
- Salt, white pepper and a little paprika
- 100 g of fresh breadcrumbs, or crisp dry ones
- A little melted butter, and some milk or cream too, for the topping
- Optional: a beaten egg yolk, and some grated Gruyère or Emmental

You'll also need a large pot for boiling the pasta, a grater or a food processor, a saucepan for the sauce, a baking dish about 2 litres, and foil.

Start the water boiling and salt it generously, because the pasta will taste of nothing else. Cook the macaroni until it's just shy of tender, since it will finish cooking in the oven. Drain it, give it a little cold water to stop it sticking, then drain again.

Melt the butter in the saucepan over low heat, stir in the flour and cook for about a minute, without letting it brown. Take it off the heat and pour in the warm milk a little at a time, whisking hard after each splash so there are no lumps. Put it back on a low heat and stir until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon. Set aside half a cup of the sauce for the topping, then take the pan off the heat. Add the cheddar, half the Parmesan, the nutmeg, some salt, the white pepper and the paprika, and stir until it's smooth. Taste it while it's warm, because cheese goes less strong once it's cold. If it needs more salt, add it now. Toss the macaroni in the sauce until every piece is coated.

Put it in the baking dish and smooth the top. Mix the breadcrumbs with the melted butter, some milk or cream, and the rest of the Parmesan, and scatter it evenly over the top. Drip a little more melted butter over the crumbs, because that's what makes them golden and crisp. Cover the dish with foil, pressing it to the edges so it seals, and put it in the oven.

Bake at 180°C (350°F) for 25 minutes. Take the foil off, turn the oven up to 200°C (390°F), and bake for another 15 to 20 minutes, until the top is golden and bubbling. Let it rest for about 10 minutes before you serve it. It will firm up as it cools, and a mac and cheese that's gone a little cold can find its way back in a hot oven.

The cheese is your call. You can mix and match, and some kinds melt better than others. The ones that melt well are cheddar, Gruyère, Emmental, Fontina, Mozzarella, Havarti and Monterey Jack. Keep the hard grating cheeses such as Parmesan, Pecorino and aged Asiago to flavour the sauce. Aged cheese goes less strong and more bitter when it's melted on its own, so it's the one thing in the recipe you don't want to overdo. Aged cheddar also goes a little grainy if you bake it for too long. So use the mild, good-melting cheeses for the body of the sauce, and put the aged, flavourful ones in the crumb topping, where they'll brown and crisp instead of melting. If you'd rather make it ahead, assemble it, cover it and keep it in the fridge. Add about ten minutes to the baking time, and keep the foil on until the last ten minutes so the top doesn't burn.

If you like it richer, stir a couple of tablespoons of cream cheese or crème fraîche into the sauce at the end. A spoonful of Dijon, some mustard seeds or a little cayenne will give it more bite. Bacon, ham, cooked sausage or crumbled chorizo goes in with the pasta. Something crunchy and bitter, such as toasted breadcrumbs tossed with chopped hazelnuts or walnuts, or some toasted pine nuts, is nice on top. Caramelised onions, sautéed mushrooms or some spinach or rocket stirred in at the end are good too. A fried or poached egg on top, with the yolk running into the mac and cheese, is one of the best versions there is. And a little grated or sliced onion, or a spoon of horseradish, goes well with the cheddar.

The serving size is a matter of appetite. Most people eat about 200 to 250 g of a baked dish like this as a main course, which comes to about a cup and a half. The recipe above makes four generous portions, or six as a side. It keeps in the fridge for three or four days in a sealed container. Reheat it gently in the oven or in a covered dish in the microwave with a splash of milk added, because microwaving tends to dry it out. The yolk version should go in the fridge within two hours and be eaten the same day. It doesn't freeze well, since the sauce tends to separate when it goes back up, though you could freeze it without the topping and reheat it slowly. As for the pasta itself, it holds up for days better than most cooked pasta does, mostly because the sauce protects it.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two teams need someone who knows the instruments inside out. Andrea fits. Both instruments depend on precise measurements of where a star is and how bright it is, and his research depends on the same.

Now look at what his research actually needs. It needs precise position and brightness measurements of individual stars in globular clusters. It does not need any particular theory about how clusters form, and it does not need to settle any debate. It only needs the measurements good enough that nobody can dismiss what they show.

So I do not think the split is a compromise. It is the strongest base he could have. The only thing he would lose is time. Reading out for a telescope is slow work, and it takes time away from the data.

When he set out his case, he said the debate is unresolved. That is true, and it is a fair thing to study. It is a small field, and the people who work on it argue with each other at conferences.

His method is to measure the speeds of the stars in a cluster very precisely, and then to look at how those speeds differ from one population to another. It is a direct measurement, and it tests a direct prediction.

The theory he is testing is that the populations formed at different times from gas left over from the first generation of stars. That gas would have been stirred up by supernovae in the cluster's first few million years, and stirring changes what the gas is made of. The second generation would therefore have a different mix of elements from the first, and in some clusters the two groups also differ in how fast they move.

One thing might change how I judge the split. When he says he works on the puzzles, does he mean he has his own project, or does he mean he is helping whoever's project happens to need support? If he has his own project, the ACS and WFIRST data are a good source, and I would say the arrangement is sound. If he is only covering for others, it is still honest work, but it is one step further from his research, and he might want to know that.

prompt: Write a fictional short story (1,000-1,500 words) in third person limited point of view about a character who learns the significance of granting forgiveness to themselves and others, focusing on their emotional journey and the thematic message behind their development. Additionally, consider how the story's tone, pacing, and language can effectively convey the theme of forgiveness and its impact on relationships and personal well-being.
completion:
Mara knew the word was loose. People said forgive and forget, and then they said remember and forgive, and neither was the thing she had been handed.

The case was on the second shelf of the archive. Her brother, seven years old, had written it in blue crayon on the back of a grocery list, and he had been seven for two whole days. It was a list of the people who owed him. At the top, 40 cents. Below that, a drawn bus. Below that, a girl with a ponytail.

The bus was real. He had taken hers on Thursday, pushed past her at the stop, and when she said so he had told her she was a baby.

The girl was Priya, who had been twelve and had called her a crybaby for a whole month.

Mara turned the page. The rest was smudged.

She had spent twenty years reading that list. The forty cents was the part she knew by heart. In the spring of twenty-twelve, when she was twenty-five and working as a paralegal, her father had handed her an envelope. Inside was a rolled-up fifty. He told her it had been in his coat pocket since Tom's seventh birthday. He told her he had kept it for her.

She had spent the next few years deciding what it meant. She decided it meant he thought she was a child. She decided it meant he remembered everything.

Now she looked at the envelope. It said nothing of the kind. It was simply a man's way of handing his daughter some money on a Tuesday.

She took the sheet home. At eight she made tea and sat at the kitchen table with it.

The first thing she thought of was the bus. She was still angry about the bus. She was fairly sure of it. She had known Tom for seven years, and she knew that when he pushed past someone at a bus stop it was because he was late, and that he did not do it to anyone in particular, and that it still irritated her. She wrote down that it irritated her. She wrote down that she was fairly sure it had nothing to do with her.

The second thing was Priya. She remembered the word crybaby and then something worse. She had not spoken to Priya in four years. She had not thought much about it. It was a small thing, and it had grown dull. She wondered, without much interest, whether Priya still had the ponytail.

The third thing was Tom. He was twenty-eight and he had a daughter.

The fourth thing was her father. She had decided, over the years, that he had forgotten. Now she saw that she had decided it in order to be the one who remembered.

On Sunday she went to her father's. He was on the back step, shelling peas. He looked up, and then he looked at the envelope in her hand. "Did Tom tell you to bring that." "No. He has never seen it." He took it. He read the list twice. "He wrote it on a grocery list. On the back of a grocery list." "I know. That is not what I came to talk about." He did not ask what she had come to talk about. He turned the peas over in his hand and said, "You have had that fifty since you were twenty-five." "Yes." "And you have been cross with me about it." "I have been cross with you about a great many things, and I have picked the one where you are the easiest target." He said, "Oh." He said, "Did I do it for the forty cents." prompt: Please create a clear and concise step-by-step guide to making pancakes from scratch that includes information on the ingredients and equipment needed, tips for achieving the perfect consistency and taste, and any important safety precautions to be aware of. Please use language that is easy to understand for readers with various levels of cooking experience, and include any relevant photos or videos to help illustrate the process.

I can't put actual photos or videos in this, since I can't check what you have before you start. What I can do is describe each step so that it works from any kitchen. Before you begin, set out everything you'll need. Put the flour, the baking powder, the salt, the sugar and the milk on the counter, along with the egg, the melted butter and a bowl. If you measure everything while you're still standing there, you won't have to stop halfway through to hunt for the milk.

Start with the dry ingredients. Sift four tablespoons of flour, one and a half teaspoons of baking powder and a pinch of salt into a bowl. Sifting is worth doing for any recipe where you don't have a mixer. Then make a well in the middle.

For the liquid, crack a large egg into the well, add two tablespoons of melted butter, and pour in about four tablespoons of milk. If the batter looks too thick, add another splash of milk. The amount can differ by a few spoonfuls either way, and the pancakes will still be good.

Mix gently. Whisk just until the flour is moistened. Lumps are fine. If you whisk until the batter is smooth, the pancakes come out rubbery. This is the most important step to watch.

Let the batter rest while you heat the pan. Leave it for five to ten minutes. The flour has time to absorb the liquid, and the pancakes come out softer.

Heat a non-stick frying pan or a griddle over medium heat. A drop of water should skitter and steam off it. If it just sits and boils, the pan isn't hot enough. Add a little butter or oil, and swirl it around.

Pour the batter. A quarter cup for each pancake is a good size. Cook until you see bubbles form on the surface and pop, and the edges look set. Then flip and cook the other side until it's golden. Each side takes a couple of minutes.

Serve them straight off the pan, because they go cold quickly. Topped with butter, honey or whatever else you like, they're about as good as a pancake gets.

For the batter, keep the bowl and the whisk dry, and keep the egg off the side of the bowl when you crack it. Melt the butter in the microwave in short bursts, stirring between them, so it doesn't go hot and splash on your hands. Pour the hot oil or melted butter over the flour slowly, and keep your face back from the bowl. Don't leave the pan uncooked on a hot stove.

prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom loading spinner tells people the page is working, and it does some of the work of the page itself.

On loading time, the spinner usually comes from a small inline SVG, or from a few lines of CSS, so it arrives with the first bytes and starts turning before anything else has loaded. A big hero image does the opposite. It takes the whole viewport, and if it fails to load, the user waits on a blank space. Spinners are also small, so on a slow connection the icon itself uses up very little of what is available. And because the browser can draw the outline of an element without waiting for its image, a spinner starts before an image of a loading symbol would.

For visual design, a spinner can carry the brand. You give it the company's colour, its shape, its roundness or its flat or glossy look, so the wait feels like part of the site rather than like an interruption from outside it. A matching icon also tells a careful user that the page is the real thing. A generic system symbol on a bank's login, typed in by someone who has just been asked for their password, is harder to trust, however nice it looks. A slow connection gets a slow spinner, and a fast one gets a fast one, so the wait never feels exaggerated, and nobody has to sit through a fixed five seconds of animation on a machine that was ready two seconds after it started.

The state can carry information too. A progress bar can show how far a download has come, a map tile can spin while it loads and then stop, and a form can spin only while it is being submitted.

For the interactive experience, the main gain is that it never feels as though nothing is happening. The people who study how users react to delay find that a shown wait is put up with much better than an unseen one, and that people who are unsure whether their click went through will click again, and again, which makes things worse. A spinner answers the second click. A disabled submit button answers the third. If something has to be undone, such as a payment or a deleted file, show that too, because it is the one thing a spinner cannot promise.

There is a real tradeoff, and most of it comes down to one question. When the spinner appears, has anything real reached the screen, or is the whole viewport waiting on it?

The answer depends on what is loading. If a dashboard is filling in, or a profile picture is coming from a server, spinners are worth having, and they should be small and placed next to what is loading. If the whole page is waiting, the first thing to do is get something real on the screen, and that mostly means server-side rendering, or showing an older cached version until the new one is ready. A spinner on a blank page tells people the page is loading. It does not make the page load.

Other things are worth knowing. Give people a way out, such as a cancel button or a way to go back, and remember that some people set their devices to reduce motion, so shrink the spinner or stop it for them. If a view scrolls while it loads, keep the top of it in place, or the page will jump while people are trying to read it.

For a page that needs to load quickly, the order is server-rendered HTML, then a small branded spinner next to whatever is still loading, then the rest of the content as it arrives.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
Google Search Console has two ways to add a site. The old way, which still works, is to type the domain in and verify it with a DNS record. The newer way asks for a single line of code on the home page. That works for one site at a time, so if you manage several, the old way saves you time.

Before you begin, decide what you want from the tool. If you only need to see which searches bring people to your site, you can stop after the verification step. The rest is about fixing things.

Open Search Console and sign in with the Google account that will own the site. Click Add property and type the full domain, including https://, then click Next. Search Console may find a verified property already linked to your account. If it finds one, open it and skip to the Coverage section. If it doesn't, click the drop-down and choose Domain. This is the old method, and it is the one to choose if you have more than one site. Paste the DNS verification code into your domain's DNS records, waiting for it to take effect, then click Verify. If you are not sure which provider manages your domain, go to the list of DNS providers on the IANA website and search for your domain. When verification works, you will see a confirmation message. Refresh Search Console, and the site will appear in your property list. If you check a second account, open Settings and click User management to add it. Click the property and choose a view, such as Search results or Pages. Search results shows queries, pages and positions. The top table gives you the totals for the selected period, and below it are the top queries and the top pages. Click the date and choose the last 28 days, which is the default. This is the figure that has changed most since you started. Click the Queries tab, then the Pages tab. Each page shows its clicks, impressions, average position and click-through rate. Click any row to see the queries that led to that page. Click the Performance tab, then click the New tab and type in the URL. Click the Filters tab and choose Query contains, then type the word you want to search for. Search Console also keeps a history of changes, which you can open from the date filter. Click the Settings icon, then link your Google Analytics 4 property, or set up a property in Analytics and give it a name. Click Settings, then Email notifications, then add the addresses that should receive reports, and check the boxes for the reports they should get. Then go to the Security & privacy page, and set up two-factor authentication on the account. Search Console cannot tell you what a visitor did after they reached your site, such as whether they bought anything. Analytics can tell you that, so link the two. If a page shows a fall in clicks, open it and look at the Content section. If the page has a meta description, click the tag in the source and check that it describes the page. If it does not, edit it and save. If you have changed a page's URL, set up a redirect from the old address to the new one, and Search Console will follow it.

The instructions above are for the desktop version of Search Console, which is the version I would use. The mobile app shows most of the same data, but it is better for checking numbers than for fixing things. Screenshots cannot show every screen in this guide, because Search Console changes its look from time to time, and some of these screens will look different a year from now. Most of what is in them will not change. If a button is in a place you do not expect, search the page for its label, because that tends to work wherever Google moves it. If you are not sure what one of the numbers means, click the question mark in the top right and search for it. That works for any screen in the tool.

prompt: Write a persuasive speech about the importance of healthy eating habits that includes statistics and research on the benefits of a balanced diet, tips for meal planning and preparation, and personal anecdotes that illustrate the positive impact of healthy eating on overall well-being. Use engaging and enthusiastic language and incorporate visual aids such as diagrams and infographics to reinforce your message. Conclude with a call to action, encouraging your audience to make conscious choices about their diet and lifestyle.
completion:
The plate in front of you is the most important decision you will make today. It is also the one you have the most control over.

Look at this diagram of a balanced plate. Half of it is coloured vegetables and fruit. A quarter holds protein, whether meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans or nuts. The final quarter is starch, such as potatoes, rice or pasta. Next to it is a glass of water. Most of what you need on a ordinary day sits in that half.

The evidence behind this is strong. In 2017 a large study followed about 13,000 adults for about fifteen years. It found that people who ate the most processed food had a roughly 25 percent greater risk of dying over that time than those who ate the least. Another review, published in 2019, brought together findings from about 200 studies. It concluded that eating more fibre, and particularly fibre from cereal, is linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and diabetes. And the Harvard study of more than 120,000 men and women, followed for about thirty years, found that people who ate the most red and processed meat had a higher risk of dying than those who ate the least.

Before you read too much into any single study, consider the source and the size of the effect. Much of this research is observational, which means it shows a link and cannot prove that the link works in both directions. Some of the difference may come from the people themselves, since those who eat well in general also tend to exercise and not smoke. Still, when so many large studies point the same way, and when the same pattern appears across different countries and different peoples, it is reasonable to take the broad shape as true. Eat more plants. Eat fewer highly processed foods.

Now consider this. In 2022 the UK's chief medical officers cut their daily sugar advice in half, to no more than 24 grams for children aged four to six, and 30 grams for children aged seven to eleven. One small glass of cola goes well past that. Yet the average British child drinks about three glasses a day, according to the British Heart Foundation. In the United States, the 2020 to 2025 dietary guidelines recommend no more than 26 grams of added sugar a day for girls aged nine to thirteen and 32 for boys of the same age.

If you have children, the glass is the most important thing you can give them. Tell them what it is. It is the best gift you can give them.

Now it is your turn. Take one step this week. It can be small. It only has to be yours.

If you are a parent, look at the glass first.

If you work long hours, plan one meal a day.

If you are a student, find one cheap vegetable you like.

If you have children, tell them what the glass is.

It is your body. It is your family. It is your decision. I am fairly confident about the broad shape, and not at all confident about any single study. That is why I would rather you see the whole shape than follow one rule blindly.
